newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: U.S. labour opposes Cambodian trade benefits.
newsitem.headline: U.S. labour opposes Cambodian trade benefits.

text.p: The AFL-CIO, the largest labour group in America, will oppose the extension of key trade benefits to Cambodia because workers' rights abuses plague the Southeast Asian nation, an ALF-CIO spokeswoman said on Tuesday.

"The AFL-CIO will oppose the granting of Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) privileges for Cambodia," said Bama Athreya, country representative for the Asian-American Free Labor Institute (AAFLI), a Cambodia-based AFL-CIO affiliate.

She said alleged incidents of child labour, forced labour, poor working conditions and a lack of trade unions meant Cambodia did not meet the labour standards required for GSP status, which Cambodia applied for in October.
The announcement comes during Cambodia's 30-day U.S. review period for GSP, a trade benefit that gives developing countries duty-free status on many exports to the U.S.

Commerce Minister Cham Prasidh earlier this month predicted Cambodia would secure GSP by year's end, but the complaints about labour rights violations could stall the nation's momentum, analysts said.

A sticking point is controversy over Cambodia's garment industry. While that sector does not stand to gain from GSP, which exempts garments, the high-profile industry figures largely in the labour debate.
Proponents of the garment sector say it provides good jobs to 16,000 workers at 34 factories, but opponents cite reports of verbal and physical abuse, poor working conditions and low pay.
Workers from Cambodia Garments, the largest manufacturer here, told Reuters they are denied overtime wages, subjected to verbal and physical abuse, and make only $35 a month.
But Pheng Rithy, a spokesman for Cambodia Garments, said the company has addressed the workers' complaints and refuted them.

Industry Minister Pou Sothirak met the company's owner recently to discuss the complaints and said he had "received a strong understanding and commitment that they will do everything they can to improve the situation."
Van Sou Ieng, head of the National Garment Makers Association and vice-chairman of Wing Tai Apparel, a factory well regarded by rights groups, said the labour woes and GSP debate were frustrating.
"There are two sides to this story," he said. "There is no more slave spirit in Asia. We need the workers and they need us."
